Name: Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif
Location: Miani Sahib Graveyard, Lahore — the survey gives no street address, tehsil, district, or coordinates; it locates the shrine only as a dedicated plot beside the graveyard, which it describes as one of the largest graveyards in Asia.
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan (born Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was his pen name/takhallus)
Events: Annual Urs (12-14 January): chadar tabdeeli, ghusl, chiraghan, Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef, Mehfil-e-Mushaira
Description:
## Overview

Darbar Wasif Ali Wasif sits within Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard, in a plot set aside beside the wider burial ground — which the field survey describes as one of the largest graveyards in Asia, holding the graves of many well-known and pious figures alongside it. The shrine holds the grave of Hazrat Wasif Ali Wasif Awan, a twentieth-century Urdu poet and spiritual teacher. It was built by his son, Kashif Wasif, after his death in January 1993, and the survey states his family has maintained responsibility for the shrine since.

## Wasif Ali Wasif — life and career

According to the survey, his given name was Muhammad Wasif Awan; "Wasif" was a pen name (*takhallus*) he took as an Urdu literary figure and poet, and he became known by the fuller form Wasif Ali Wasif. He was born on 15 January 1929 in Shahpur, Khushab District. His father, Muhammad Arif, was himself a teacher. The survey states his family belonged to the Khushab region and the Awan tribe, whose lineage (*shajra nasab*) is said — by the family's own account, as recorded here — to trace back to Hazrat Ali (R.A.); this is reported as stated, not independently verified.

He began his education in Khushab, passing his middle-school examination there in 1939. His father then sent him to his maternal grandfather in Jhang, a move the survey describes as transformative: his grandfather had been associated with the Muslim League and had spent time with Quaid-e-Azam. In Jhang, he passed Matriculation in 1944, Intermediate in 1946, and his B.A. in 1948, all from Government College Jhang and all in the first division. He went on to Government College Lahore for his M.A., and passed the Civil Services examination in June 1954. The survey states he was offered a government post on the strength of this but declined it, turning instead toward writing and solitary devotion.

He founded an institution called "English College" in Anarkali, Lahore, which the survey describes as a gathering place for people of every background, where free food (*langar*) and offerings (*niyaz*) were continuously distributed, and where he began guiding visitors and devoting himself to their concerns. He later addressed large public gatherings — the survey specifies "over a thousand nights" of addresses at Lakshmi Chowk and Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, taking questions on both spiritual and worldly matters.

## Writing and teachings

The survey states he wrote more than 50 books, poetic compositions, poems, ghazals, and *na'at*, in both Urdu and English, and names a number of them: *Ghumnam Adeeb*, *Kiran Kiran Suraj*, *Qatra Qatra Qulzum*, *Harf Harf Haqeeqat*, *Mukalma*, *Dil Darya Samundar*, *Ba Say Baat*, *Dareche*, *Zikr-e-Habib (S.A.W.)*, *Guftagu*, *Shab-e-Chiraagh*, *Shab-e-Zaat*, *Baray Barwey*, and *The Beaming Soul*. The survey records a saying attributed to him: "You and I are equal; we must please our Lord, and one day we all have to return." It describes his teaching as combining devotion to the Prophet (recitation of *na'at*) with an explicit call to patriotism — that people owed a debt of gratitude for their homeland alongside their duties to God.

## Why the shrine is significant

The survey reports that people regard him as a pious servant of Allah who gave his life to serving others, and who fulfilled requests made of him without exception. It states that both Muslims and non-Muslims visit the shrine and study his books, and that gatherings held in his name draw poets, scholars, teachers, and writers. Because he is described in the survey as having died in this devoted state, visitors are recorded as regarding him as a martyr (*shaheed*) in the sense of one who remains, in the survey's words, "forever alive with Allah" — a status the survey attributes to popular belief rather than to any formal religious ruling.

## Devotional life and the annual Urs

Free food (*langar*) is distributed daily, and visitors come to make offerings (*niyaz*), pray, and recite Fatiha for him; his books are kept at the shrine for visiting scholars to read. Gatherings called Mehfil-e-Mustafa (S.A.W.) are also held there. The annual Urs is observed every year on 12, 13, and 14 January, with the ceremonial changing of the shrine's cloth covering (*chadar tabdeeli*), ritual washing (*ghusl*), lamp-lighting (*chiraghan*), gatherings in praise of the Prophet (*Mehfil-e-Naat Shareef*), and poetry gatherings (*Mehfil-e-Mushaira*), attended by scholars and devotees; the survey notes that non-Muslim attendance at the shrine is also common. The survey estimates 1,000-1,200 daily visitors, rising to roughly 150,000-200,000 during the Urs. Opposite the shrine is a private library where visitors gather to read and buy his books.

## Custodianship

The shrine remains under the management of Wasif Ali Wasif's family. The survey states that offerings (*hadiya*) collected there fund its ongoing upkeep and construction work, and that devotees take part in caring for it directly.

## A note on the source wording

The survey's answer on sect/spiritual lineage reads, verbatim: "Kandan Kabila, Ahl e Sunnat, Awaz belong in past with Hazrat Ali (R.A), Baithi Hazrat Shah Niyaz Ahmad Chisti Qadri." This appears to intend something like: Awan tribe (*qabila*), Ahl-e-Sunnat, a claimed lineage back to Hazrat Ali (R.A.), and spiritual allegiance (*bai'at*) to Hazrat Shah Niyaz Ahmad Chishti Qadri — but the phrasing as recorded is not fully grammatical and is reproduced here rather than silently cleaned up, since resolving it further would mean guessing at what the surveyor meant.

Name: Darbar Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami
Location: Miani Sahib Graveyard, Lahore, Punjab. The field survey places the shrine "in the middle of Miani Sahib Graveyard" but gives no street address, no locality/section name within the graveyard, and no coordinates.
Sufi Saint: Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami
Events: Annual urs (date not stated in the survey); recurring mehfil (zikr-e-Ilahi and Naat-e-Rasool) every few days; Thursday lamp-lighting (diyas) and vow-making (manatein)
Description:
## Overview

In the middle of Miani Sahib Graveyard in Lahore — one of the city's great burial grounds — stands the shrine of Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din Gharib Nawaz Chishti Nizami, a Chishti Nizami Qadria saint remembered above all for a generosity so unstinting that he was called *Sakhi Lajpal*, "the generous one who never turns anyone away." The field survey that is this entry's only source gives no street address, no named section of the graveyard, and no coordinates — only that the shrine sits within Miani Sahib's grounds, surrounded on all four sides by the graves that make up the wider burial ground.

## The Life of Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din

The survey is explicit that Hazrat Khawaja Feroz-ud-Din was his real name — not a title conferred later. It gives his birthplace as Kandhari Bazaar, in the Rang Mahal quarter of Lahore, and names his parents: his mother, Mehtab Bibi, described as an exceptionally devout woman who raised him carefully, and his father, Hassan Din, a poor and hardworking man already connected to the Chishti Qadria order, whose labour left him little time to oversee his son's education directly. On his birth year, the survey is genuinely unclear rather than silent: it states he was "born in the latter part of the 1900s (19th century)" — a phrase that contradicts itself, since the 1900s and the 19th century do not refer to the same decades. No other figure for his birth is given anywhere in the survey, so his birth year is left here as the source leaves it: stated, but internally inconsistent, and not resolvable from this material alone.

Coming of age, he pursued the righteous path on his own initiative. At fifteen he pledged allegiance (*baith*) to Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa Chishti-Nizami — an event the survey records as arriving through a dream, in which his future spiritual master appeared to him and said, "Your share is with us; come and take your share." He woke the next morning and travelled to his master's seat of learning on Barki Road, Lahore, to complete the pledge in person.

He never left his father's trade: the survey describes him working as a shoemaker in Rang Mahal Bazaar for the whole of his life, making and selling shoes, while living with deliberate simplicity. His nights, from Tahajjud until Fajr, were given to the remembrance of Allah; his days to his shop and, increasingly, to the stream of people who came to him. His spiritual master at one point asked him to visit only on Fridays rather than daily, out of concern for the length of the journey Feroz-ud-Din was making to reach him.

## Pledge of Allegiance and Succession

According to the survey, all of his religious learning came from his one spiritual master and guide, Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa Chishti-Nizami, whom he served closely for the rest of the older man's life. When Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa died in 1390 AH, he called Feroz-ud-Din to him in his final moments, conferred on him the cloak of succession (*khilafat*), and named him his spiritual successor. Thousands are said to have pledged allegiance to Feroz-ud-Din after he received this khilafat. He continued, the survey states, to mark his own master's annual Urs with honour throughout his life, without wanting elaborate invitation or attention drawn to the observance itself — a preference for a low profile that, per the survey, extended to his everyday manner: he asked disciples to visit on Fridays but treated anyone arriving on another day with the same humility.

He died suddenly of a liver ailment on Friday, 27 November 1981, and his disciples built his shrine at Miani Sahib, where — the survey says — a crowd of visitors is present at all times.

## The Shrine

The survey describes the shrine itself as built "very beautifully," using expensive marble and fine materials throughout its construction. Inside, it houses rare relics associated with sacred personalities from around the world, which his disciples are said to have brought back, preserved, and put on display over time — a detail the survey offers as part of what gives the shrine its splendour, distinct from the devotional life described below. The wider graveyard surrounds the shrine on every side.

## Devotional Life and the Annual Urs

A spiritual gathering (*mehfil*) — combining the remembrance of Allah (*zikr-e-Ilahi*) with praise of the Prophet (*Naat-e-Rasool*) — is held every few days, together with free food (*langar*). Thursdays draw people specifically to light lamps (*diyas*) and make vows (*manatein*). The survey estimates daily footfall at 750 to 1,000 visitors.

The annual Urs, per the survey, includes lamp-lighting, large-scale langar, the changing of the shrine's ceremonial cloth (*chadar tabdeeli*), ritual washing (*gusal*), further mehfilein, qawwali, and sustained zikr-o-azkar — drawing, the survey estimates, some 175,000 to 225,000 pilgrims. The survey does not, however, give the calendar date on which the Urs falls, despite describing its observances in detail.

A reciprocal relationship binds this shrine to that of Feroz-ud-Din's own master: his disciples attend Hazrat Khawaja Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa's Urs in large numbers, and in turn the disciples of Sheikh Muhammad Mustafa take an active part in organising Feroz-ud-Din's own Urs — a link the survey attributes to the scale of the following Feroz-ud-Din drew in in his own right after receiving khilafat.

## Custodianship

The shrine is maintained, per the survey, by his special disciples (*mureedeen-e-khas*) and their descendants, who took over its administration immediately after his death and continue to run it today; some workers are privately employed to attend to the shrine at all times.

Name: Darbar Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri
Location: Miani Sahib Graveyard, Lahore. Per the field survey, this shrine is the oldest seat within Miani Sahib Graveyard — the graveyard grew up around it over the centuries, not the reverse. The survey gives no street address, no coordinates, and no position within the graveyard's roughly 475 kanals beyond "alongside the mosque" that Hazrat Tahir Bandagi built.
Events: Annual Urs (7th-9th Muharram): Mehfil-e-Naat and langar, deliberately without dhol or dhamal per the current custodians' account of the saint's own wishes. Weekly Mehfil-e-Naat and langar on Thursday nights and Fridays.
Description:
## Overview

In Lahore's Miani Sahib Graveyard -- by local report the largest graveyard in Asia -- the oldest seat belongs not to the dead in general but to one man in particular: Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri, a scholar and Qur'an-teacher who built a mosque, a madrasa, and a library on this ground while he was still alive, and who was buried beside his own mosque when he died in 1630. The graveyard, according to the shrine's own field survey, grew up around his tomb over the following centuries, as generation after generation asked to be laid to rest near him -- not the other way around.

## The Life of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi Qadri

He was born in Lahore in 1576 CE. His father, Fazlullah, gave him his early education, and he went on to memorize the Qur'an. For advanced learning he became a disciple (*mureed*) of Hazrat Shah Sikandar, who is credited with giving him the name "Tahir Bandagi" -- telling him, as the survey records it, "you are meant for the spiritual reformation of people; simply remain devoted to the service of humanity at all times."

The survey also preserves an episode presented as a real trial in his life: a period in which he became enamored of a Hindu woman and stepped back from his religious work. His well-wishers are said to have appealed to Hazrat Mujaddid Alf Sani on his behalf, after which he returned to his path and formally became Mujaddid Alf Sani's disciple as well -- later teaching Mujaddid Alf Sani's own children. The survey reports this plainly, as part of his story rather than something to smooth over.

In his later years he married twice -- to Mah-e-Khanam and to Ismatullah, the survey noting the latter as the daughter of an Afghan king -- and spent his nights, by the same account, absorbed in remembrance (*zikr*) rather than in the comforts that came with his following. He is described as periodically fasting and practicing self-denial for stretches of fifteen to twenty days, and as never allowing the crowds who gathered around him to produce pride.

He died on 8 Muharram 1040 AH, which the survey gives as 8 August 1630 CE -- the two calendars agreeing exactly -- at the age of 54, consistent with the birth year of 1576 the same survey states.

## The Mosque, Madrasa, and Library

The land that is now Miani Sahib Graveyard was, in Hazrat Tahir Bandagi's lifetime, gifted to him so that he could teach. On it he built a mosque, a madrasa, and a library (*kutub khana*), and taught the Qur'an there himself. The survey records one specific episode from this period: Sikh raiders, believing gold was hidden inside boxes on the premises, broke in and found only books -- and, on discovering this, threw the books back into the locality and left. When Hazrat Tahir Bandagi died, his resting place beside this mosque became his shrine, and rulers and disciples of the period are said to have kept it under careful administrative care from the start.

## Legends and Disputed Accounts

Several traditions are attached to the shrine, and the survey is candid that not all of them are agreed on even by today's visitors.

One account holds that Hazrat Tahir Bandagi, while leading Taraweeh prayers, was granted a vision of the Prophet Muhammad, who told him that whoever looked upon him, learned from him, or was buried near him would enter Paradise -- offered as the reason so many notable figures chose burial around his tomb.

A second, more contested tradition concerns jinn. The survey records that graves near the shrine are popularly said to belong to jinn who watch over the site, and that some visitors report having seen figures in human form vanish before their eyes. But the survey is explicit that this is not universally accepted even among visitors: others say that although the graves exist, they have never personally witnessed any jinn or wild animal there, and regard the jinn stories as ignorance -- pointing out, in their own study of Hazrat Tahir Bandagi's life, that he himself never taught or endorsed such beliefs. Both positions are recorded by the survey as live, current opinions, not settled fact.

## Why the Shrine Matters to Visitors

The survey attributes the shrine's continuing importance to answered prayer across generations: families who saw their petitions answered here return, and bring their children to do the same. Hazrat Tahir Bandagi is described by visitors as a "perfect saint" (*wali-e-kamil*) who was granted visions of the Prophet and of other venerable elders on multiple occasions, and the presence of Jinnat and of other noble burials nearby is offered by devotees as further evidence, in their eyes, of his spiritual standing.

## Devotional Life

A mosque stands beside the shrine where the five daily prayers are held, and visitors come both for prayer and to recite the Fatiha and make personal supplications. The survey notes that some families have visited for generations, following parents and grandparents before them. The main recurring gatherings are Mehfil-e-Naat and langar, held weekly on Thursday nights and Fridays.

Daily attendance is given as 1,200 to 1,600 visitors.

## The Annual Urs

The Urs falls every year on the 7th, 8th, and 9th of Muharram, drawing an estimated 250,000 to 300,000 pilgrims across the three days. The current custodians (*Gaddi Nasheen*) describe Hazrat Tahir Bandagi as someone who did not care for drumming (*dhol*) or ecstatic dance (*dhamal*), and say the Urs is kept accordingly restrained -- centered on Mehfil-e-Naat and langar rather than music or dancing.

## Custodianship

The shrine is overseen today by its Gaddi Nasheen (current custodians), with several people formally employed as staff who, per the survey, consider caring for the shrine year-round to be a privilege rather than a job.

Name: Darbar Ghazi Ilm Din Shaheed
Location: Miani Sahib Graveyard, Lahore. The field survey itself locates the shrine only as “Lahore” (its one detail, ‘Railway Auqaf land,’ refers to the funeral prayer, not necessarily the burial site); the placement at Miani Sahib comes from published press accounts — see Bibliography. The pin is the graveyard landmark, shared with the other Miani Sahib entries, not the grave's exact position.
Events: Annual urs (31 October: chadar-changing, gusal, Mehfil-e-Naat, langar, collective prayer); Thursday-night Mehfil; daily lamp-lighting and vow-making
Description:
## Overview

In Lahore lies the shrine of Ghazi Ilm Din Shaheed, a young carpenter revered across Pakistan not as a Sufi master or spiritual guide but for a single act: the killing, in 1929, of the publisher of a book judged blasphemous against the Prophet Muhammad. The field survey that is this entry's only source describes a shrine visited daily for prayer, vow-making and intercession, and calls him *Ghazi-e-Millat* and *Fakhr-e-Ummah* -- "warrior of the nation" and "pride of the community."

## Family and Early Life

According to the survey, Ghazi Ilm Din was born on 4 December 1908 in Lahore to a family of carpenters (*tarkhan*); his father's name is given as Taleh Mand. He had two brothers, one a fellow carpenter and one a government employee. The survey describes the family as widely respected by neighbours for its piety, with no history of dispute with anyone. Ilm Din received an early education at a neighbourhood madrasa before entering the family trade.

## The Blasphemy Case, as the Survey Narrates It

The survey dates the origin of the case to 1928, when a Hindu publisher named Rajpal issued a book, *Rangeela Rasool*, that the Muslim community of the time considered blasphemous. It states that a British magistrate sentenced Rajpal to only six months' imprisonment -- judged far too lenient -- and that a further appeal, heard by a magistrate named Dalip Singh, secured Rajpal's release on bail, further inflaming public anger. Two earlier attempts on Rajpal's life are recorded in the survey: on 24 September 1928 a man named Khuda Bakhsh tried and failed, and was sentenced to seven years; later a man named Abdul Aziz, said to have travelled from Afghanistan, struck the wrong man (Swami Satyanand, not Rajpal) at Rajpal's shop, and received fourteen years.

The survey then describes Ilm Din overhearing a public gathering recounting Rajpal's offence, and reports a dream in which an elder rebukes him for sleeping while his Prophet is insulted -- a dream his friend Sheeday says he shared the same night. The two are said to have drawn lots three times to decide who would act, with Ilm Din's name emerging each time. On 6 April 1929, per the survey, Ilm Din went to Rajpal's shop and killed him, then walked to Anarkali police station and turned himself in without expressing regret.

*Note: this entire episode is presented here exactly as the field survey states it -- the surveyor's own retelling of a well-known historical case, not checked here against other historical accounts of the same events.*

## Trial and Execution

The survey states that Muhammad Ali Jinnah represented Ilm Din at the High Court, and advised him against confessing so a defence could be mounted; Ilm Din is quoted as refusing, calling the killing the one deed of his life he took pride in. The High Court passed a death sentence on 7 July 1929, which the survey says Ilm Din welcomed, preferring the gallows to imprisonment. It states that Jinnah and Allama Muhammad Iqbal both sought clemency from the British government without success, and that Ilm Din was executed at Mianwali Jail on 31 October 1929.

## Funeral and Burial

The survey describes the body brought from Mianwali to Lahore under tight security, with funeral prayers led by Qari Shams-ud-Din, Imam of the Wazir Khan Mosque, on Railway Auqaf land, attended -- per the survey -- by an estimated 600,000 people. It states that Allama Iqbal and Allama Mehr-ud-Din Londkhori lowered the body into the grave, and quotes Iqbal as saying, on that occasion, "this carpenter's son has surpassed us all."

## Why the Shrine Is Venerated

The survey reports that visitors regard Ilm Din's act as proof of a station high enough that Allah answers prayers made through his intercession (*waseela*). It also records an account, attributed to elders who visited him in prison, that the Prophet appeared to him nightly to recite the Qur'an -- including an episode with the visiting scholar Pir Syed Meher Ali Shah, in which Ilm Din is said to have corrected a lapse in Meher Ali Shah's recitation of Surah Yusuf, prompting Meher Ali Shah to liken his imprisonment to that of the Prophet Yusuf.

## Devotion and Events

Per the survey, people come daily -- an estimated 400 to 600 visitors -- to light lamps, make vows (*mannat*), recite Fatiha and distribute langar; a space for two to three prayer rows sits beside the shrine. Thursday nights bring a dedicated Mehfil. The annual urs falls on 31 October (the date of the execution) and includes Mehfil-e-Naat, chadar-changing, ritual washing (*gusal*), langar, and collective prayer.

## Custodianship

The survey states the shrine is managed by a body called the Ghazi Ilam Din Shaheed Committee, with some matters handled by the Auqaf Department. It separately notes -- as a point some visitors raise -- that Rajpal was the book's publisher, while various accounts describe its author as an anonymous or pseudonymous figure, distinct from Rajpal himself.
